title: Landscape-scale conservation

definition.text: An approach that manages a whole landscape to balance nature conservation against farming, forestry and other economic uses of the same land.

facts.text: It is an alternative to protecting single sites.
Its backers argue that poverty, food security, climate change, water scarcity and biodiversity loss are linked, so they need coordinated action across a landscape.
A river basin, for example, supplies water, timber, crops and habitat, and each use affects the others.
Rather than serving a single land use, it tries to meet the interests of many different stakeholders.
The IUCN applied it in 27 landscapes in 23 countries.
Often called the landscape approach, it was described by UNEP in 2015 as embodying ecosystem management.
Landscape approaches try to meet several Sustainable Development Goals at once, for example raising farm output, flood defence, biodiversity and carbon storage within one river catchment.
A review found five barriers, including confusing terminology, long delays before action, and sectors working in silos.

notes: Also covers the syllabus phrase concept 'Landscape approach' (phrase-working-lands), which the sources use as a synonym; no separate entry drafted.

definition.text: A way of managing a landscape sustainably by bringing together stakeholders who want different things from the land.

facts.text: Sara Scherr coined the term in 2012 for planning whole regions rather than single farms or plots.
By 2016 it had five steps: stakeholders meet, share information, plan together, carry out the plan, and monitor and adapt.
It seeks synergies among conservation, farm production and rural livelihoods.

title: Sustainable agriculture

definition.text: Farming that reduces harm to the environment, maintains and builds up natural resources, and uses non-renewable resources productively.

facts.text: Agriculture has a huge environmental footprint; food systems cause one third of human greenhouse gas emissions.
It aims to produce crops or livestock without damaging soil, water, biodiversity, or the people on and near the farm.
Its elements can include permaculture, agroforestry, mixed farming, multiple cropping and crop rotation.
In 1977 the USDA defined it as practices that, over the long term, meet food needs, improve the environment, use resources efficiently, keep farms viable and improve farmers' quality of life.
Environmental costs left out of a farmer's ordinary accounts are called externalities.
Investment in it is said to be four times more cost-effective than direct food aid, yet gets only three percent of humanitarian funds.
Many certification systems exist, including organic certification, Rainforest Alliance and Fair Trade.
People disagree on its definition: an ecocentric view favours low growth and organic methods, a technocentric view relies on technology and modified industry.

contested_note: Sources describe a debate over how to define sustainability in agriculture, between ecocentric and technocentric views.

definition.text: Farming methods that raise production while also improving environmental outcomes, without clearing more land.

facts.text: It differs from earlier intensification by putting weight on broader environmental results.
By 2018 an estimated 163 million farms in 100 nations used it, on 453 million ha, equal to 29% of farms worldwide.
Whether ecosystem services can replace non-renewable inputs while keeping yields high has been much debated.
In east Asian rice fields, nectar plants that support pest predators cut insecticide need by 70% with a 5% yield gain.

definition.text: A strategy that keeps farmland and nature strictly apart, farming some land intensively for high yields so that other land can stay wild.

facts.text: It has been the dominant strategy in developed countries for over 150 years.
Reviews find it generally favoured for conserving tropical forest biodiversity, in 67% of relevant studies.

definition.text: A strategy, also called wildlife-friendly agriculture, that makes room for biodiversity inside farmed areas by farming less intensively.

facts.text: Agroforestry and mixed crop-livestock systems are examples.
Reviews more often find it better for food security and livelihoods, in 58% of studies.

title: Land sparing versus land sharing

definition.text: The long scientific argument over whether nature is better protected by separating farms from wild land or by mixing them.

facts.text: The debate has run for over a decade without a clear consensus.
Sparing tends to win for tropical forest biodiversity, sharing for food security and livelihoods.
A third option, land blending, has been proposed because each strategy's success depends on the landscape.

contested_note: Scientists have debated the two strategies for over a decade with no clear consensus.

definition.text: An in-between strategy that mixes land sparing and land sharing to suit each landscape.

facts.text: It only recently emerged as a credible alternative; research suggests it can reconcile conservation and farming while building resilience.

definition.text: Farming focused on the environmental side of sustainable agriculture, using methods that rebuild ecosystem services.

facts.text: It aims to prevent erosion, improve water infiltration, store carbon as humus and raise biodiversity.
Techniques include no-till farming, multispecies cover crops, strip cropping, terraces and shelter belts.
Crop genetic diversity lowers the risks of monocultures, which can be vulnerable to a changing climate.

title: Multifunctional agriculture
article: Sustainable agriculture#Different viewpoints about the definition

definition.text: The view that farming does more than produce food and fibre, also managing renewable resources, conserving landscapes and supporting biodiversity.

facts.text: It is a farm-centred lens that treats these other functions as outputs of farming.
The rival ecosystem-services lens instead starts from benefits nature gives people, such as pollination, soil formation and nutrient cycling.
